This paper investigates map-based code-representation workflows as a design variable in agentic software engineering, examining how different repository views change agents' retrieval behavior, task success, token use, and latency.
  In this paper, we study five code-representation workflows: abstract syntax trees, call graphs, module dependencies, documentation-enriched search, and a hybrid workflow that combines them. Each workflow exposes a repository map that the agent can query during a task. We evaluate Claude Code with Haiku 4.5 against a raw-tool baseline on four repository-level tasks: fault localization with LinuxFLBench, repository-level code generation and repair with SWE-bench Pro, test generation with SWT-bench, and security patching with SecBench.
  The results show that representation workflows are most useful as token-saving tools when localization is the bottleneck, while their success gains narrow when the decisive step is patch or test authoring. On LinuxFLBench, all five workflows improve recall@10 over the baseline (0.757-0.829 vs. 0.717) and reduce token usage by 25-39%. On SWE-bench Pro, resolution remains close to the baseline (44.3-50.6% vs. 49.0%) while token usage drops by 17-26%. On SecBench, Callgraph has the highest patch-resolution rate in this sample (34.3% vs. 28.9%) and uses fewer tokens, but all workflows increase latency. On SWT-bench, Hybrid and Docs have the highest reproducing-test rates in this sample (47.8% and 47.2% vs. 44.7%), but all workflows use more tokens and take longer. Overall, map-based workflows change both what the agent inspects and how much it spends, but their benefits are task-dependent rather than universal.

title: Robust Ranking of Port Impacts from Impending Tropical Cyclones: A Two-Stage Recommendation System
summary: When a tropical cyclone (TC) threatens several ports, preparedness planning depends on anticipating which ports are likely to be affected and where disruptions may last longest. Limited historical observations at individual ports and uncertainty in landfall location make these relative impacts difficult to estimate. We use a two-stage recommendation framework that first selects candidate ports based on their proximity to the expected landfall location and then ranks them by their estimated number of impact days. Using AIS-derived impact days for 37 ports and 31 TCs in the Gulf of Mexico study region, we compare three ways of representing port--cyclone interactions: pairwise feature interactions, tree-based feature combinations, and explicit feature crosses combined with learned embeddings. In tests on Hurricanes Nicole and Ian, the retrieval stage consistently identifies all observed affected ports under landfall uncertainty. Among the ranking models, Wide & Deep Learning achieves the closest agreement with the observed port rankings. Its mean ranking agreement exceeds that of the distance-based baseline by 85.5% for Nicole and 55.5% for Ian and is less sensitive to uncertainty in the landfall location. These rankings could help port authorities prioritize post-cyclone inspections and allocate recovery resources across ports threatened by the same event.

title: Decision Models as Retrieval Gates Against Injection and Pollution
summary: Retrieved web text can carry instructions aimed at the language model, or synthetic pages written to mislead. We test whether released open-weight decision models, which answer typed questions about a text without generating tokens, can screen retrieved passages against both threats. On a benchmark of 1,000 questions over forum-style web pages with hidden injected instructions, a Kev-4B gate reads each passage's HTML. Attack success, measured automatically, falls from 27.9% with no defence to 13.6% with the published mitigations (sanitisation, normalisation and citation prompting) and to 5.7% with the gate added. The gate takes 76 ms per passage and wrongly flags 4 of 186 benign pages with instructions for human readers. Responsiveness on clean queries stays within a point (85.6% to 86.2%). On a 200-query pollution testbed where two thirds of the candidate pages are fake, filtering the pool before the top ten are chosen keeps fake pages out of the answer (0.5% exposure) and holds accuracy at 83%, against 28% with no filter. Filtering only the top ten leaves the generator too few pages to answer. Large LLMs used as judges rank attacks better (AUROC 0.99 against 0.94) but cost ten times more. Gates catch more attacks when they read the page's HTML than when they read its plain text. Every model is open-weight.

title: Take It From Here: Evaluating Coding Agents On Project Takeover
summary: Coding agents increasingly collaborate on long-term projects. When taking over a project, they need to recover currently applicable requirements from the interaction history and update them in response to new requests. However, most coding benchmarks do not include long interaction histories, and some evaluations that consider history still do not cover the full process from requirement reconstruction to project delivery. We therefore provide agents with the interaction history, current request, and pre-request project environment, ask them to make the requested changes, and assess takeover performance through delivery tests. Across six model-harness configurations and 37 targets eligible for executable validation, the mean complete-delivery rate under Full History is only 4.95%. We then use requirement atoms to independently diagnose a larger set of takeover targets, examining relevant information identification, pre-request state reconstruction, and current request processing. We further supply correct pre-request or target states to examine the remaining difficulties in requirement processing and project modification. The diagnostics show that none of the six configurations produces fully correct post-request requirement states, and a case illustrates omission of previously recovered constraints during updating. With correct target states supplied, the mean complete-delivery rate is 8.11%, with build and regression pass rates of 96.40% and 90.99%, but target-test success remains 9.01%. These results show difficulties in both forming target requirement states and implementing supplied targets in existing projects. Based on these findings, we introduce ReqMemBench, which combines requirement diagnostics with delivery validation to support systematic evaluation of project takeover.

title: EnvOpt: Automated Optimization for Agent Environments
summary: An LLM agent's cost and success depend on its model, its harness, and its environment. In addition to the widely studied directions of parameter tuning and harness optimization, we propose the third direction: optimization over stationary environments. Agents are often deployed in rich environments shared by many tasks, such as a company's Slack workspace or a complex collection of data sources, documents or tickets. We call these environments stationary environments. We introduce EnvOpt, a method for automated end-to-end optimization of stationary environments for any given model and harness, using real or synthetic tasks without needing any graders or reference answers. On AutomationBench, EnvOpt reduces the cost of Claude Haiku 4.5 by 72.7% and raises its pass rate by 14.34%. The same environment transfers to Opus 5, cutting its cost by 68.1% with a 1.34% gain. Added on top of Meta-Harness's optimized harness for Haiku 4.5, it lowers cost by a further 83.4% and adds 11.17% accuracy over Meta-Harness alone. Across 5 benchmarks, EnvOpt significantly reduces the cost of agents while improving or maintaining pass rate, and is transferable to different models and different harnesses. We also discuss common successful and rejected environment optimization strategies during automated optimization. More broadly, our results show that how information is represented to an agent shapes both its cost and its success, making the environment worth optimizing in addition to the parameters and the harness.

title: LABBA: LLM-Assisted Behavioral Biometric Authentication
summary:
Behavioral biometrics have emerged as a promising complement to traditional physiological biometrics by leveraging dynamic human characteristics. These modalities offer advantages including continuous authentication, inherent liveness detection, and greater resistance to credential theft and other spoofing attacks. However, existing systems remain limited in adaptability, contextual awareness, and semantic reasoning as they primarily rely on similarity metrics, static thresholds, or supervised classifiers. As a result, they often struggle with real-world conditions such as behavioral variability, environmental changes, contextual changes, and adversarial manipulations.
  To address these limitations, we systematically integrate LLM-based contextual reasoning into behavioral biometric authentication. LLMs provide capabilities in contextual inference, sequential reasoning, multimodal understanding, and adaptive decision-making. Building on these strengths, we integrate a lightweight LLM-based reasoning module with a novel phone-blowing behavioral biometric technique to develop a context-aware authentication framework. To this end, we first collect blow-acoustic signals from participants and systematically extract spectral and temporal features. These features are aggregated and converted into comparable similarity representations, using either discrete rule-based categories or continuous normalized scores, which are transformed into structured prompts through prompt engineering.
  We experimentally evaluate the proposed framework using blow-acoustic data collected from 50 participants under diverse behavioral and contextual conditions. The proposed framework achieves 99.46% and 99.38% authentication accuracy in the rule-based and score-based modes, respectively, outperforming its non-LLM counterpart while maintaining strong robustness under dynamic real-world conditions.

title: Req2Rust: A Requirements-Guided Agent Harness for Project-Level C++-to-Rust Migration
summary: Memory-safety concerns make Rust an attractive target for modernizing legacy C/C++ systems, yet project-level C++ migration must balance semantic fidelity with Rust-oriented reconstruction. Source-structure-preserving migration can track low-level behavior, but it can also carry source-language organization, unsafe idioms, and project assumptions into Rust. Direct agent-based translation gives the model more freedom to construct a Rust project, but semantic coverage depends on the model identifying the source behaviors that must be preserved. This problem is especially acute for C++, where source behaviors are often hidden in object models, destructor-driven lifetime protocols, and other hard-to-localize C++ semantics. This paper presents Req2Rust, the first project-level LLM-based C++-to-Rust migration harness. Req2Rust first derives an evidence-grounded Migration Requirements Specification (MRS) that records the behaviors and constraints that must be preserved. It then synthesizes a Rust Design Specification (RDS) and realizes it as an initial Rust project. Because real projects contain implementation details and idioms that only become visible during build and validation, Req2Rust treats the initial Rust project as an executable refinement state. Compiler, semantic, and unsafe-reduction validators produce validation reports for improving buildability, behavioral alignment, and unsafe usage. We evaluate Req2Rust on general C++ projects and modules from the large-scale Openharmony codebase against a ClaudeCode baseline. Req2Rust produces buildable Rust crates in both settings and improves test pass rate from 69.5% to 91.9% on general projects and from 45.4% to 87.9% on Openharmony modules.

title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance
summary: Language agents increasingly work for users on the open Web, and finance is where trusting them is hardest. The data must come from the Web, the strategy lives in the user's head, and correctness depends on time, so an agent can fail silently: a strategy the user never asked for, unverified data, or a backtest that uses the future yields a report as convincing as a correct one. Existing benchmarks close the world somewhere, fixing the task, the data, or the timeline, and thereby remove these failures instead of measuring them. We introduce FINCOSMOS, an open-world evaluation paradigm for agents doing financial work. A simulated user holds a hidden strategy sampled from a compositional grammar and reveals it only when asked. The agent receives no data, so it must acquire data from the Web, build its own backtest under a data cutoff, and deliver verifiable results. Grading needs no reference answer. Programs verify point-in-time correctness and recompute every reported metric, the delivered strategy is checked against the hidden specification, and a run is accepted only when the user is satisfied and none of 15 veto checks fails. Across four coding agents and a model without tools in 150 sessions, no session is accepted: every session that the simulated user signed off fails a program check, and agents raise only 54--64\% of the details they were not told. Human experts attribute 88.33\% of failures to the agents. With FINCOSMOS feedback, an agent with persistent memory learned all ten tasks.

title: SensorGuard-RV: Sensor-to-Register Data Protection for Resource-Constrained RISC-V Devices
summary: Embedded systems rely on sensor measurements that traverse a complex hardware-firmware stack (e.g. peripheral interfaces, communication buses, memory, and drivers) before reaching the applications that use them. At worst, an attacker with access to this path may successfully intercept, overwrite, fabricate, or replay readings. This may cause systems that act on such data, such as flight controllers and industrial processes, to behave incorrectly or unsafely. Existing defences, such as trusted execution environments and trusted I/O paths, still depend on trusted driver software and correctly configured access control, which remain fragile in practice. In response, we present SensorGuard-RV, a hardware-first approach that delivers sensor samples into processor registers without trusting intermediate software, buses, or memory. After configuration, a write-once ownership switch hands the sensor to a fixed-function controller that performs hardware-level authenticated encryption on sensor samples under a key inaccessible to software. We develop a new RISC-V instruction then instructs the CPU to decrypt the sample and writes it to a register only after verifying its tag and rejecting replays, including across resets. We implement SensorGuard-RV on the NEORV32 core with an ADXL362 SPI accelerometer on an Artix-7 FPGA. At 100 MHz, a protected sample reaches a register in 5,191 cycles (51.9 $μ$s), of which the two Ascon authenticated encryption engines account for 30. Because fixed-function acquisition removes per-byte software polling, the protected loop sustains 19,015 transactions/s, 5.3% above a software-driven SPI baseline. The added logic (3,155 LUTs and 2,215 registers; 5.0% and 1.7% of the device) is dominated by the Ascon engine and preserves the 100 MHz clock, while estimated power rises from 118 to 368 mW.

title: Route Before Response: Fail-Closed Routing for LLM-Enabled Customer-Service Software
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Accepted to the 33rd Asia-Pacific Software Engineering Conference (APSEC 2026). Code and data: https://github.com/YgcCoder/RouteBR
summary: LLM-enabled customer-service software in financial institutions must choose a downstream service before responding. Classifiers and LLM routers can identify a relevant label or destination, but a composed application must still verify dispatch permission and entity registration. We study this integration problem as boundary-aware pre-response routing. We present RouteBR, a controller in which one model call proposes a primary service action and registered object, then deterministic code checks identifiers and versioned rules before dispatch or a specified non-dispatch outcome. Lower-ranked candidates cannot replace a blocked primary route. We construct 600 privacy-preserving scenarios from recurring confidential-request patterns at a real financial institution; three engineers jointly reviewed the scenarios and labels. On the 200-case CONFIRM MAIN split, RouteBR reaches 97.5% final-path exact match. A matched one-call baseline given the same rules reaches 95.5%, whereas a diagnostic baseline without the rule program obtains 94.0% action accuracy but only 41.0% final-path exact match. Across 166 non-dispatch MAIN and FLIP cases, RouteBR produces no false dispatch. The artifact pairs all 1,960 prediction rows with raw receipts while excluding gold and reviewer fields from model requests. These results support separating model proposals from code-owned, replayable execution. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/YgcCoder/RouteBR.

title: SAVeR$^2$: Reasoning-based Safety Alignment for Large Reasoning Models via Verifiable Rewards
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved impressive performance via explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet this process introduces critical safety risks. We formalize LRM safety objectives as requiring non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency, and explicit intent identification. We argue that existing alignment methods suffer from poor adversarial generalization, a significant ``safety tax'' on reasoning, and unfaithful coarse-grained rewards, primarily due to their neglect of the LRM's intrinsic reasoning capabilities for safety. To address these, we propose \textbf{SAVeR$^2$}, a novel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{A}lignment method via \textbf{R}ewards with \textbf{R}easoning capability. SAVeR$^2$ decomposes the safety objective into four fine-grained verifiable reward signals and utilizes a difficulty-aware data selection strategy to stabilize training. Crucially, we introduce a reasoning-preserving gradient projection mechanism that analytically resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients, effectively eliminating the safety tax. Extensive experiments on models ranging from 1.5B to 671B demonstrate that SAVeR$^2$ achieves superior safety performance and significantly lower over-refusal rates across multiple benchmarks without compromising general reasoning capabilities.

title: FedReason: Large Language Models as Weight-Space Meta-Aggregators for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. It analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only the printed results, may score a few candidates on a 500-image proxy set, and submits a short Python aggregation program. The server applies the program until the next call and falls back to FedAvg whenever its output is invalid. Full weight tensors never leave the server. We evaluated FedReason with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines. Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It was the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but did not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious, it excluded all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stayed about one point below FLTrust without training a root model. Without proxy feedback, accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed. A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.

title: Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities
summary: Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this experience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver, an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution to support experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses. We evaluate Evolver using Claude Code and Codex, two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-rebench, and GAIA. On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions, Evolver improves task success from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points) while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%. Furthermore, among 265 pairs successful under both conditions, token consumption decreases by 17.57%, demonstrating efficiency benefits even when task success is preserved. These findings suggest that persistent procedural experience can improve both task effectiveness and execution efficiency, providing a practical foundation for transforming agent exploration into evolving capabilities.

title: DelegateEval: Evaluating Platforms for Personal External Service Agents
comment: 28 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Evaluation framework and experimental design
summary: AI agents that work for an individual over time may also help that individual serve external clients. We define a personal external service agent as an agent authorized and continuously managed by a specific individual to accept client requests, deliver work, and provide ongoing support using that person's knowledge, experience, professional methods, and service boundaries. Such agents could allow individuals to serve more clients with less direct involvement and generate economic value at scale. We propose DelegateEval, a platform-level evaluation framework for agent systems that may combine large language models, reusable skills, protocols such as MCP, and executable tool environments. It covers eight dimensions: ease of creation, service discovery and matching, delivery quality, expertise inheritance, service continuity, learning and improvement, reliability and governance, and efficiency and value. These dimensions assess whether a platform enables people with different backgrounds to turn their expertise into ongoing services that deliver verifiable work, develop capabilities through experience, and remain economically feasible. We present the framework and an experimental design. Complete datasets, executable environments, a unified scoring protocol, and cross-model results remain to be developed and empirically validated.

title: SoK: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Integration in Software Development: Approaches, Gaps, and Future Directions
summary: Standardised post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is critical for protecting software systems against future quantum threats, but standardised algorithms alone do not provide a pathway for their secure integration into software. This paper presents a Systematisation of Knowledge (SoK) of PQC integration in software development, synthesising existing approaches across implementation, migration, and developer education. We analyse these approaches against NIST PQC standards and PQC migration guidance, software development lifecycle coverage, cybersecurity practices, deployment maturity, and testing and evaluation evidence. Our analysis shows that existing work establishes important technical and organisational foundations but provides disconnected support across the software development lifecycle, with limited coordination between preparation, implementation, migration, deployment, maintenance, and developer practices. Evaluation evidence also remains concentrated in controlled or early-stage settings, providing stronger evidence of technical feasibility than operational readiness. We identify cross-cutting gaps and research directions for developing lifecycle-oriented, empirically validated approaches that connect technical, developer, and organisational requirements for secure PQC integration.

title: AiXapply: Fast and Reliable Full-File Code Integration with Specialized Small Models for IDE Workflows
summary: Large language models increasingly assist developers by proposing small code edits, yet reliably integrating a partial update snippet into an existing file while preserving unrelated content remains poorly supported by current code-generation workflows. We formalize the Code Integration (Apply) task as follows: given an original file and an update snippet, the system must produce the complete merged file while preserving all content outside the requested edit. We construct a high-quality multi-language dataset from real commits via a structured pipeline that converts code changes into update snippets paired with full-file ground truth and enforces consistency through verification and filtering. We then train a specialized 4B model, aiXapply, using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (GRPO). The supervised variant achieves 94.4% accuracy under our language-aware comparison, surpassing a strong large-model (Deepseek-V3.2) baseline (91.6%). Speculative decoding enables aiXapply-RL to reach $\sim$2700 tokens/s on a single A100 in a decoding subset; on the full benchmark, it achieves roughly 75$\times$ lower latency than the API-served Deepseek-V3.2 baseline. We further conduct an industrial deployment of aiXapply-RL in the aiXcoder IDE plugin as a dedicated Apply service, reducing mean Apply latency from 50 seconds to 1.89 seconds by offloading full-file generation from the upstream large model. Under time-based capacity planning, replacing one of five upstream serving instances would save 20% of upstream machine cost before the additional shared A100 service cost. Overall, our results demonstrate that treating code integration as a standalone task enables small models to achieve high accuracy, practical efficiency, and concrete industrial benefits in real-world IDE workflows where latency, cost and privacy are critical.

title: Graph learning-assisted logic-based Benders decomposition for distributionally robust in-station train rescheduling under disruptions
summary: Uncertainty in resource reopening times complicates train holding and rerouting decisions when resource closures coincide with arrival delays and processing-time extensions. We develop a rolling-horizon distributionally robust model that updates predictions of the remaining closure duration as observations of disruption resolution become available. The model jointly optimizes train routes, sequences, and timings. It minimizes the worst-case expected total completion delay over an ambiguity set of scenario probabilities. The solution algorithm, GNN-LBBD, uses logic-based Benders decomposition to coordinate routing and resource scheduling. Conditional cuts are constructed from resource-use patterns, and a graph neural network guides the order in which resource relaxation subproblems are solved. Across 28 test instances for a five-track station, GNN-LBBD achieved a mean total completion delay of 61.13 train-min. This was 16.63\% lower than tabu search and 20.06\% lower than variable neighborhood search, with a mean total computation time close to that of tabu search. Information comparisons on six representative instances showed that using observations of disruption resolution reduced mean total completion delay by approximately 21.7\%. Scenario-based and conditional-mean predictions produced similar overall results under the same information conditions. The benefits of information were more pronounced in some instances with alternative routes. This suggests a relationship between the use of observations, the station resource structure, and the scope for schedule adjustments.

title: What the Middleman Delivers: Answer Behavior, Tool Permissions, and Billed Usage in LLM API Relays
summary: Third-party application programming interface (API) relays offer access to large language models (LLMs), often at lower prices. Users depend on these services for model quality, instruction compliance, and accurate billing. However, existing studies leave unclear whether relays meet these expectations together. We test 20 relays offering GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5. First, we compare answers to knowledge questions with batch-matched official responses. In our first-round sample, the analysis flags 7/10 low-price and 2/10 same- or higher-price relays for behavioral differences. On retesting 35 pairs, seven gain or lose a flag under the original rules, and six under matched correction families. Because answer comparisons cannot reveal every delivery problem, we examine returned content and tool permissions. No injection is confirmed in 3,332 screened responses to a fixed, non-adversarial code and setup workload, yet four relays return tool calls despite instructions disabling them in the first round. Finally, to connect reported usage to actual costs, we compare input-token counts with official references and check balances. For identical requests, five relays report 4,200 to 60,000 more input tokens than the official API. Where balances are available (six services), charges follow reported usage at listed prices, including extra reported input tokens at one service. Our study shows that advertised models and prices are insufficient to judge relay reliability. It identifies unexplained billed token quantities and tool-permission violations as risks and shows why service evaluations need repeated measurements.

title: Goal-Branching LaCAM: Temporary Goals as Search Branches in Dense Multi-Agent Pathfinding
summary: LaCAM is a search-based solver for multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF) that runs a depth-first search over joint configurations, using PIBT to generate successors and lazily adding single-agent constraints to explore alternatives. Although LaCAM is complete, it can struggle on dense, corridor-heavy instances because extracting blocking agents from deadlocks requires coordinated moves of several agents, often away from their goals, which PIBT's greedy one-step successors rarely propose and which LaCAM can only reach by enumerating constraints one agent at a time. This paper proposes Goal-Branching, where blocking agents are given temporary goals, each tried as an additional branch of LaCAM's search. We examine random and corridor-aware rules for choosing these temporary goals and show that completeness is preserved for any such rule. On dense instances (60-90% of free cells occupied) of three maze and room maps, Goal-Branching solves 89% of instances against 44% for LaCAM*, and, on instances both solve, it finds a first solution 10-14x faster on maze-32-32-2 and room-32-32-4, and nearly 200x faster in median time at 75% density on room-32-32-4. Solution cost increases by 15-22% on instances both solve, while on open maps and the full MovingAI benchmark its solutions cost no more than those of LaCAM* and it is at most 3% slower.

title: Fix One, Miss Another: Leveraging Historical Bug Fixes to Uncover Residual Bugs in Database Systems
summary:
Database management systems (DBMSs) implement SQL constructs through grammar-driven dispatch handlers. Although handlers for syntactic siblings implement different SQL constructs, they often share a common implementation pattern, including argument extraction, type checking, and permission validation. Consequently, a bug fix that hardens the handler exercised by a historical bug may leave the corresponding logic in sibling handlers vulnerable to the same semantic flaw. We refer to such defects as sibling bugs. Despite the structural similarity among sibling handlers, existing bug-finding techniques rarely exploit historical fixes to systematically uncover these related defects.
  We present Reaper, a novel approach for detecting sibling bugs guided by historical bug fixes. Reaper first analyzes a bug fix to infer a trigger profile, which characterizes the conditions under which the defect is exposed, and a validation profile, which captures the semantic evidence needed to distinguish buggy behavior from correct behavior. It then projects the trigger profile onto syntactic siblings through grammar-guided test mutation, generating tests that exercise corresponding semantic paths in sibling handlers. Finally, Reaper validates suspicious behaviors using the inferred validation profile through a staged validation process, reducing false positives caused by complex DBMS behavior.
  We evaluate Reaper on four widely used DBMSs, including MariaDB, MySQL, OceanBase, and CockroachDB. Reaper uncovers 61 previously unknown bugs, of which 57 have been confirmed by developers and 13 have been fixed at the time of writing. These results demonstrate that historical bug fixes contain actionable semantic knowledge that can be systematically transferred across syntactic siblings to uncover otherwise overlooked defects.

title: CST-Bench: Benchmarking Counterfactual Spatial Transition Reasoning with Causal Transition On-Policy Self-Distillation
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables; includes technical supplementary material
summary: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing benchmarks mainly focus on static scene understanding. When objects are moved or swapped, models must infer not only spatial relations but also how interventions change the scene state. To address this problem, we introduce CST-Bench, a benchmark for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CST-Bench contains 7,082 examples covering 6 intervention types and 12 transformation operators, with dense causal annotations including intervention sources, affected relations, expected effects, invariant relations, and metric changes. We benchmark general-purpose MLLMs on CST-Bench and further compare post-training strategies on CST-Bench and standard spatial benchmarks. Results show that methods effective for ordinary spatial reasoning can still fail under counterfactual interventions. We further formulate counterfactual spatial reasoning as causal state-transition modeling and propose CT-OPSD, which uses CST-Bench annotations to guide a teacher model in learning counterfactual state transitions and causal reasoning chains. These chains are then distilled into a student model that reasons only from real observations. Overall, experiment results establish CST-Bench as a challenging benchmark and reusable supervision resource for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CT-OPSD further provides an initial demonstration of how its annotations can support model improvement.

title: Uncovering Systematic Blind Spots in Graph Database Testing through Integration and Process-Level Analysis
summary: Graph databases are becoming foundational infrastructure for connected data, and a growing body of automated testing techniques has uncovered many bugs across mature graph database systems. Each technique checks a different aspect of correctness and exposes a different class of defect. Combining them is the natural next step, but each technique is judged by the real bugs it finds, not by useless reports or tests that can never fail, and that is what decides whether a developer can afford to fix the problems. To identify the remaining gaps, we integrated test capabilities from 8 testing methods and conducted an empirical study of their behavior, during which we found two blind spots. First, 12 hours of testing produce thousands of bug reports, far more than the number of genuine defects a mature database is likely to contain. Most reports are false positives caused by dialect or pattern-matching differences, and many of the remaining reports are duplicates. Second, analysis of process-level data reveals that many equivalence-based metamorphic test cases lose their ability to detect defects because of the optimization mechanism. Based on these findings, we summarize and realize these guidelines in GraphWeave, an integrated testing platform for graph databases. This includes a multi-agent system that analyzes the flood of bug reports to produce gating rules for issue filtering and adapter rules for dialect adaptation, and a plan-aware triage routes metamorphic pairs by plan, skipping those that share a plan on the same graph state and therefore cannot detect defects. We apply GraphWeave to NeuG, a recently open-sourced industrial graph database that has not been covered by prior graph database testing work. With modest manual effort, GraphWeave uncovers 19 previously unknown bugs, all of which have since been confirmed.

title: FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving
summary: In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/tree/releases/v0.30.0.

title: ReConMem: A Graph-Based Dual Memory System for Repository-Oriented Conversations
summary: LLM-based code assistants are increasingly used in iterative repository-level development, where effective assistance requires jointly leveraging evolving conversational history and repository context. Existing memory systems, however, are primarily designed for general-purpose conversations and do not sufficiently coordinate conversational information with the structured code entities to which it refers. We propose ReConMem, a graph-based dual memory system for repository-oriented conversations. ReConMem organizes distilled conversational memories and conversation-relevant code entities into interconnected semantic and structural memory graphs, while maintaining their cross-graph associations as interactions evolve. For memory recall, ReConMem combines natural-language and code-aligned retrieval through code-draft-based query grounding, expands retrieved information over intra- and inter-graph relations, and compresses retrieved code according to its structural granularity. We evaluate ReConMem on two repository-oriented conversational benchmarks spanning long-horizon context management and realistic project-grounded multi-turn assistance. On LoCoEval, ReConMem improves Pass@1 over the strongest baseline by 7.917 and 7.292 percentage points on single-hop and multi-hop subsets, respectively, with comparable context compression. On CodeAssistBench, it achieves 27.61% Correct and 44.03% Partially Correct, exceeding Full History by 4.10 and 7.09 percentage points, respectively, while improving interaction quality. These results demonstrate that aligning conversational memory with repository structure improves context management for repository-oriented multi-turn interactions.

title: Align Before Aggregation: Basis-Consistent Federated LoRA under Heterogeneous Ranks
summary: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) under heterogeneous client capacities is increasingly important, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with heterogeneous ranks makes it practical. Existing server-side aggregators compose local matrix updates $ΔW_i$ from client-specific LoRA factors $(A_i,B_i)$ before aggregating them. Although these matrix updates lie in the same weight space $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and can be averaged directly, the LoRA factors that generate them may expressed client-specific local basis. In the typical compose--aggregate--factorize--dispatch loop, this basis inconsistency can make the rank-$r_i$ reference prefix dispatched to lower-rank clients unstable after server-side refactorization. In this work, we propose \textbf{FedAbA}, a basis-consistent federated LoRA aggregation framework for heterogeneous ranks. FedAbA first extracts each client's local basis, aligns it to the corresponding prefix of the global reference basis, and constructs a basis-consistent reconstruction of each local matrix update before aggregation. It then aggregates these reconstructions with weights that combine client data size and consistency score, followed by exact coefficient-space SVD refactorization and gauge fixing before rank-prefix dispatch. Our theoretical analysis clarifies the role of basis consistency and supports the proposed consistency-aware aggregation mechanism. Extensive experiments show that FedAbA outperforms representative federated LoRA baselines, with the largest gains under the strongest rank heterogeneity.

title: Fast Unsupervised Anomaly Detection Methods on Software Logs - An Empirical Study
summary:
Anomaly detection on software logs ensures system reliability through failure identification, root cause analysis and fault localization. While supervised models show excellent performance, in a practical setting there rarely are labeled training data available. This calls for the use of unsupervised models. We study effects of data preprocessing, anomaly detection method, and the dataset. For preprocessing, we examine three options: The use of anomaly-free training data, using randomized as opposed to chronologically selected training data, and the use of a custom loader to extract log message from the log line. Regarding anomaly detection we use four models (KMeans, IsolationForest, RarityModel, Out-Of-Vocabulary Detector) and three representations (Words, trigrams, and parsed events). We evaluate these approaches on seven datasets: BGL, HDFS, Hadoop, Spirit, Thunderbird, Liberty, and LO2Token. We run each combination of the selected factors and measure performance with AUCROC and F1-score metrics. Then we utilize a generalized linear model to establish relationships between the factors. Furthermore, we address execution times.
  Our evidence reveals large variability across all datasets, preventing us from making recommendations that apply universally. For instance, log parsing enhances performance on some datasets but reduces it on others. The evidence suggests that using anomaly-free data for training unsupervised models can improve anomaly detection performance, though this requires extra effort to identify such data.Previous work has argued that shuffling data leads to unrealistic model performance (data leakage). Yet, our results show this does not hold for the unsupervised models we tested, while it remains true for supervised models in the same setup. For fast execution of the pipeline, use word representation and avoid IsolationForest model.

title: Embedding-Space Fingerprinting of LoRA Fine-Tunes: Recovering the Training-Data Domain from the Model Artifact Alone
summary: When a base language model is fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), how much of the training data domain leaks into the resulting artifact? This paper studies whether a simple classifier can recover the domain of a fine-tune given only the model artifact (weight deltas, internal activations on a fixed probe set, or generated text) without ever observing the training data. Using one base model (Qwen3.5-0.8B), 36 LoRA fine-tunes are produced over 18 public datasets in five domains (medical, code, mathematics, non-English text, narrative prose), and three feature families are extracted at decreasing levels of access: white-box weights, gray-box activations, and black-box outputs. A leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) protocol, frozen before any result was seen, tests whether the domain of a fine-tune trained on a previously unseen dataset can be identified. The domain is recoverable well above chance (20%) from gray-box activations (61%) and black-box outputs (64%); white-box weight statistics reach 42%. Contrary to the pre-registered hypothesis that signal decays monotonically from weights to activations to outputs, activations and outputs were more informative than the weight-delta statistics. The black-box result holds unchanged (64%) when only generated text is used, without token probabilities. Domain accuracy is also stable when a third run per dataset is trained on an independently drawn data subsample, and black-box predictions are unaffected by the LoRA rank (8-64). All code and per-run feature vectors are released.

title: Adapt the Object to the Subject: Representative Study Material for Empirical Software Engineering
summary: External validity is a central concern in empirical software engineering, yet the debate has largely focused on whether study participants are representative. How well the study objects they reason about - code, models, or requirements - are representative of each participant's own work is often overlooked. Practitioners' own artifacts would be ideal, but are often out of reach, so researchers sample from public datasets or construct objects artificially. Whether this lack of subject-object fit affects participants' ability to act on the material remains unknown. We take a first step toward answering this question for requirements. We propose an approach that uses an LLM to generate context-adapted synthetic requirements just-in-time during an online survey from a short, participant-supplied context description, optionally injecting requirements smells as controlled stimuli. To validate the approach, we conducted a controlled experiment with 31 industry practitioners in a 2x2 design that crosses stimulus generation (static vs. synthetic) with quality (clean vs. smelly). Each participant rated the perceived representativeness and assessability of 20 requirements. Using Bayesian data analysis within a statistical causal-inference framework, we find that perceived representativeness has a strong positive effect on assessability. Synthetic requirements are rated as more representative and, primarily due to this gain, more assessable than static ones sourced from public datasets; smell injection leaves both perceptions unchanged. Our results support treating a lack of study-object representativeness as a first-class validity threat and position context-adapted synthetic study objects as a practical addition to the empirical methodology toolbox.

title: Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution
summary: Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select, analyze, mutate, and gate, achieving the best performance.

title: Which Signals of Code Correctness Survive Distribution Shift? Hidden-State and Causal Predictors of Program and Verdict Correctness
summary:
Large language models increasingly judge code, yet without external feedback such judgments are unreliable, and verifying them by executing tests or by extended reasoning is costly. Instead, execution-free correctness predictors use signals from the model's output probabilities, sampled solutions, or hidden states to identify judgments that warrant further verification. However, these predictors may degrade under distribution shifts when generalizing across projects and languages.
  We compare six execution-free predictors from four families on Qwen3-Coder-30B and gpt-oss-20b under benchmark shift between LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench and language shift across Python, C++ and Java. We evaluate two targets: whether the model's own verdict on a program can be trusted, and whether the program itself is correct. Besides established approaches, we adapt two novel causal localization methods to code, which have been shown to be more robust out-of-distribution on natural language tasks. For verdict correctness, causal localization improves robustness to language shift. For Qwen3-Coder a probe on the causally localized subspace stays 0.09 AUROC ahead of output confidence under language shift (0.11 in distribution), significantly outperforming the best non-causal predictor by 0.04 AUROC on average. This advantage, however, does not generalize consistently to gpt-oss or to benchmark shift. For program correctness, predictors transfer more successfully between benchmarks, largely by identifying problems on which the model tends to fail. However, their ability to rank candidates within the same problem is limited.

title: Redacting Personal Data: A Speed and Accuracy Comparison of Regex, Presidio and Hybrid Designs
summary: Many enterprise projects now pass free text to large language models (LLMs), and that text often contains personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, phone numbers, email addresses, home addresses and dates of birth. Once a prompt is sent, this data is copied into provider systems, application logs and observability traces. Redacting PII before the call is an obvious control, yet teams seldom have numbers on what it costs in latency or what it lets through. This paper compares four redaction designs that any LLM pipeline can adopt: a pure regular-expression (regex) redactor, Microsoft Presidio running on a spaCy model, a hybrid in which Presidio finds only person names while regex handles structured identifiers, and a fast hybrid that calls spaCy's named-entity component directly. All four share a known-entity rule, which removes the person the system already knows it is handling, and a consistent placeholder scheme, so the LLM can still tell one person from another after redaction. We evaluate the designs on a sample workflow, which we call ProfileAssist, that turns resumes into structured profiles, using 100 synthetic resumes (523 characters on average, with 900 PII values and 600 business terms that must survive). Regex ran at a 0.20 ms median but caught only 88.9% of PII, because it cannot find names that are not known in advance, such as the references listed in a resume. Presidio, hybrid and fast hybrid each caught 100% of PII and kept 100% of business terms, at median latencies of 37.59 ms, 30.23 ms and 13.48 ms. Measured against a 9,120 ms median LLM call, even the slowest option adds only 0.41% to the request. We therefore recommend the fast hybrid as a default for LLM pipelines that handle personal data, with regex kept as a safety net rather than as the only control.

title: Compositional Loop Invariant Inference for Multiphase Programs via Structured Neurosymbolic Reasoning
summary: Loop invariants are essential for deductive program verification, yet automatically inferring them for {multiphase programs}, whose loops contain conditional branches that induce multiple execution phases with distinct behaviors, remains an open problem. Existing LLM-based methods either reason about loops as a whole or use explicit branch information to generate atomic assertions jointly across branches, without maintaining complete candidate sub-invariants for independent generation and targeted repair. We present CLOVER, a structured neurosymbolic reasoning framework for multiphase invariant inference built on two interlinked mechanisms. First, compositional inference: CLOVER statically decomposes a loop into symbolic {loop branch sequences}, conjunctions of the loop guard and branch conditions that characterize distinct execution scenarios, and guides the LLM to generate candidate sub-invariants for each one independently, so that each LLM query focuses on a single execution scenario rather than the entire loop. Second, counterexample-guided localized refinement: when SMT verification rejects a composed disjunctive invariant, CLOVER traces the counterexample back through the branch structure to identify which specific loop branch sequence caused the failure and repairs only that sub-invariant, preserving all correct components. Both mechanisms are unified by a shared symbolic structure derived from the loop's branch semantics, which guides what the LLM generates, how candidates are composed, and where refinement is directed. We evaluate CLOVER on 316 linear arithmetic, 50 nonlinear arithmetic, and 54 multiphase benchmarks. CLOVER solves 35 of 54 multiphase benchmarks, outperforming the best LLM-based baseline (29) by 20.7\% and the best traditional method (22) by 59.1\%. On linear/nonlinear benchmarks, CLOVER remains competitive, solving 355 of 366 programs overall.

title: Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign, Auditable, and Deterministic Capability Execution for Logical Systems
comment: 51 pages, 26 figures. Code repository and benchmarks available at https://github.com/arpahls/skillware
summary:
Current autonomous logical systems rely on a fragile assumption: that language models should dynamically write code, guess API payloads, and memorize operational constraints through prompt engineering. In practice, this burns massive context windows, inflates API bills, and produces brittle agents that fail unpredictably in production.
  In this work, we present Skillware, an open architectural framework and capability registry that formally separates what an agent wants to do from how that task is executed. Instead of prompting models with loose text instructions or markdown files baptized as 'skills', Skillware equips them with modular, versioned software capability bundles. Much like skill hotkeys in video games that execute deterministically under fixed world rules, each bundle combines a typed JSON input contract, deterministic Python code, task directives, bundled datasets, and automated unit tests. In-process adapters translate these capabilities into native tool declarations for any model, from frontier cloud APIs to local open-weight runtimes with zero network latency.
  Evaluating 23 frontier and open-weight models across 368 benchmark conditions, we show that small local models (3B to 8B parameters) equipped with Skillware consistently outperform unequipped frontier models on complex multi-step workflows. They cut token usage by up to 84.8%, slash inference costs by up to 97.3%, and eliminate parameter errors entirely. True agent reliability does not come from larger models or longer prompts, but from equipping logical systems with verified, deterministic software.
  Finally, we articulate the trajectory of capability bundles across an invariant continuum of information processing systems: from digital logical systems today, to IoT, drones, and embodied robotics tomorrow, establishing a foundation for auditable, real-time capability execution.

title: A Low Similarity Score Does Not Show Independence after Source-Conditioned Repository Rewriting
summary: Maintainers sometimes cite a low token-similarity score as evidence that an LLM-assisted rewrite of a copyleft project is independent of the original. We test what such a score can support under \emph{source-conditioned} rewriting: a coding agent keeps the original in its working copy, rewrites the repository, and iterates until a fixed behavioural harness passes, with no human edit to the code. On 69 rewrites of six copyleft Python projects we find that: \ding{182}~Agent-only rewriting is inexpensive and often yields low scores. Every controlled rewrite passes the harness after repair, usually within half an hour for the initial rewrite. Under a ground-up rearchitecture prompt, most rewrites fall below 25\% JPlag similarity and still pass the harness. \ding{183}~A single low score is an unreliable witness. Identical project--agent--prompt configurations produce wide spreads in similarity; run-to-run variation dominates project and agent effects, and in more than a third of configurations the three repeats straddle the threshold. Rewrites retain more of the original's imports and fingerprint facts than unrelated projects do, yet hand-written independent implementations of the same task often retain as much, and neither signal separates the two groups better than chance. Thus a low score on one rewrite is weak evidence of independence: another run of the same agent may score high. Claims based on similarity should report repeated generations, and candidate provenance signals should be checked against same task independent implementations, not only against unrelated projects.

title: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
summary: Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space. We introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with organized large-scale exploration. Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and, together with expert-developed skills, supports research decisions. Self-Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents inheriting research context and decision-making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies. We introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, comprising 121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks assessed with expert-defined process rubrics. PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, autonomous investigations generated findings subsequently supported by human-executed experiments. For LpxH, PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site and screened compounds against it, identifying a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding. For JAK1, it prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity. Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self-Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome and identified a new binding target, with the interaction subsequently confirmed experimentally. PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.

title: Requirements Nobody Wrote Down: Emergence in a Public-Sector ML Pipeline
summary: Governments increasingly use machine learning (ML) to handle data volumes beyond their analytical capacity, yet little is known about how requirements arise and evolve as an ML experiment moves toward operational use. Requirements Engineering (RE) for ML often assumes that requirements can be elicited upfront; in the public sector, however, demands arrive vague, stakeholders speak different professional languages, and what counts as a ``good'' result is unknown in advance. We report a 15-month case study of a thematic classification pipeline for Brazil's national digital participation platform, which holds over 60,000 citizen proposals, triangulating 43 project artifacts with interviews of six project participants. Institutional demands arrived as broad goals, endorsed but not sponsored, and only 40\% of the 95 reconstructed requirements and criteria were ever formalized. The pipeline's key requirements emerged largely from experiments, model outputs, and integration work, shaped by technical decisions and institutional constraints; the central one, the classification categories, was settled by a government taxonomy chosen for its institutional legitimacy. Acceptance relied on technical metrics, domain judgment, and political assessment, without shared thresholds or validation of usefulness in practice. In public-sector ML, technical and institutional artifacts thus act as elicitation instruments, and experimentation and integration belong to the requirements process.

title: Who Should Know What? Empirical Information Design for Multi-Agent LLM Economies
summary: The performance of multi-agent LLM systems depends not only on the capabilities of the underlying models but also on information-sharing policies, which govern what information each agent observes and at what level of detail. But does providing AI agents with more detailed information always improve collective outcomes, or can transparency paradoxically degrade efficiency? To investigate this, we introduce empirical information design, an experimental framework that systematically compares disclosure policies across economic markets populated by LLM agents, while holding interaction rules and models fixed. We evaluate ten frontier LLMs in multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining, and double auctions, using ground-truth utilities to decouple identified opportunities from realized outcomes. We find that finer information disclosure yields highly model-dependent results. In trade, revealing exact valuations rather than ordinal preference rankings reduces realized gains for GPT-6 Sol (from 98% to 91% of maximum) yet increases them for Claude Sonnet 5 (from 72% to 86%). In bargaining, exact information leads Grok 4.7 to produce less balanced agreements, whereas Claude Opus 5.5 divides gains symmetrically. In double auctions, full disclosure inflates price demands, triggering market breakdown and lowering welfare for Gemini 3.1 Pro (97% to 78%), Claude Opus 5.5 (94% to 64%), and Grok 4.7 (97% to 62%). Overall, these results suggest that model selection and information design must be co-optimized, as LLMs vary in how their strategic responses to information impact system objectives.

title: RouteAlign: Aligning Task Requirements with Model Profiles for LLM Service Selection
summary: LLM service selection requires performance evidence that reflects the demands of the current task. Aggregate scores obscure differences in capability and difficulty, while semantically related examples can involve different combinations of skills. We present RouteAlign, which uses task requirements to structure both the measurement of model performance and the selection of services. Task requirements describe capability demand and difficulty, enabling alignment with corresponding model performance measurements. Historical requirements determine how outcomes contribute to global profiles and local capability estimates; incoming requirements determine how those measurements inform the current decision. A shared scorer integrates the evidence, and a generation-cost preference controls selection among eligible services. Evaluation across diverse tasks and heterogeneous LLM services shows that RouteAlign extends the empirical quality-cost frontier toward higher task quality. Comparisons with open Jev-style decision backends show consistent quality gains, with lower generation cost than their strongest tested configuration. Ablations support the contribution of local performance evidence, while catalog-update experiments demonstrate effective reuse of the fitted scorer with refreshed model measurements.

title: MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents
summary:
Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction.
  We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone.
  We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at https://github.com/J1zz/mcp_hallu.

title: Accepted but Wrong: Silent Failures of LLM Code Repairs after API Migrations
comment: 30 pages, 2 figures. Preregistered; artifacts are available from the authors on request
summary: After a runtime or API migration, an LLM-repaired procedure can run cleanly yet return wrong results, and a release check on typical test inputs ships it. We report a preregistered study of 73 tasks covering 60 documented changes in CPython, Node.js and SQLite. Every candidate is executed on the real runtimes against withheld contracts. Over the complete repair space, the all-assertions gate on typical inputs released 0.410 of wrong repairs. One edge input written from the release note cut this to 0.065, and to 0.061 on 15 unseen clusters. Three inputs from a blind GPT-5.6-luna writer that never saw the program reached 0.070. Two further frozen stages enlarged the menu to 1491 fragments and then added 233 hard distractors that match the legacy output on typical inputs. The edge input (0.058) and the frontier-model writer (0.058) passed their preregistered tests. Yet 0.168 and 0.153 of the hard wrong programs still passed. Two local-model writers failed their preregistered tests. Across four model families, the edge input cut wrong releases per attempt in all three open-weight families on all three menus, for example from 0.233 to 0.057, without lowering correct completion. Self-tests helped less. A blind AI audit flagged 34 contracts as stricter than their requirements. Dropping the disputed checks changed 0 verdicts, but class-label disputes remain open. No model-written code was executed. Artifacts are available from the authors on request.

title: Towards Generalist Graph-Level Anomaly Detection
summary: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) aims to identify graphs that deviate significantly from the majority. While recent advances have achieved competitive performance, existing approaches mainly follow a dataset-specific paradigm, requiring substantial in-domain data and training cost when applied to new application scenarios. This limits their scalability and practicality in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce and diverse domains are continuously emerging. In this paper, we investigate the problem of generalist GLAD, which seeks to learn a single unified model capable of detecting anomalous graphs across multiple domains with minimal supervision on the target data. This problem introduces key challenges, including learning transferable patterns from heterogeneous graph datasets and effective adaptation under limited supervision. To address these challenges, we propose GenGLAD, a generalist GLAD approach that leverages discriminative subgraph extraction as the core mechanism to learn transferable anomaly knowledge and enable efficient adaptation to new domains. Specifically, GenGLAD employs a graph neural network-based discriminative subgraph extraction model to learn the anomaly-discriminative substructures that distinguish anomalous and normal graphs across diverse domains. During the test-time adaptation phase, multi-dimensional discrepancies between the extracted subgraph and multi-level contextual information are calculated to characterize anomalies from multiple perspectives. For efficient adaptation, a lightweight scoring module is introduced to automatically decide the most informative signals, improving robustness against misleading patterns. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves strong performance, superior generalization ability, and improved data efficiency compared to existing methods.

title: Hard Issue, Weak Model, or Bad Run? Rethinking Failure Prediction for Coding Agents
summary: Trajectory-based failure predictors for software engineering (SE) agents read the partial trajectory of a run to flag whether it is going right or wrong. If it is going wrong, the run can be stopped, retried, or switched to another model. We ask whether these predictors learn anything about the run itself. On public SWE-bench Verified trajectories, where each model attempts each issue once, two run-independent factors dominate predictor performance. The first is issue difficulty: a reference score that never looks at the run, only at how hard the issue is for other models, reaches 0.92 AUROC, whereas trajectory predictors reach about 0.62. The second is model ability: within an issue, knowing which model ran predicts failure better than our predictors do, and the predictors largely reproduce the overall ability ranking of the models. Beyond difficulty and ability, what predictors gain from the trajectory is statistically equivalent to zero. This confusion carries over to the actions taken after a prediction. Model switching is often motivated by the gap between the best single model's resolution rate and an any-model oracle. This gap is no larger than random variation alone produces. Per-issue switching gains nothing on held-out runs. In a repeated-run pilot, the same model often solves an issue in some runs and fails it in others. Retrying thus has real room to repair failures, but it rescues only failures caused by a bad run, not those on an issue beyond the model's ability. Current predictors cannot tell the causes apart, as they mostly predict the issue and the model, not the run. We call for failure prediction that explains why a run fails, evaluated on repeated-run benchmarks and in closed-loop, equal-budget settings.

title: Pediatric ECG foundation model via adult-to-pediatric fine-tuning: downstream tasks and clinical evaluation
summary: Pediatric electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation is complicated by age-dependent electrophysiological changes that limit direct transfer of adult AI models. We asked whether an adult ECG foundation model could be adapted to pediatric ECGs. Using 339,563 12-lead ECGs from 238,189 children, we compared direct application, pediatric fine-tuning, and training from scratch under an identical architecture. Direct transfer was poor (mean AUC 0.8256). Fine-tuning reached 0.9695, above de novo training (0.9661), and attained 0.9079 using only 1% of training data. On 10,999 external ECGs, fine-tuning achieved a mean AUC of 0.9385 across 30 labels. It generalized to age regression (MAE 1.12 years) and congenital heart disease classification (AUC 0.9562). Across 17 clinicians and 100 cases, diagnostic accuracy rose from 56.8% to 65.4% (p < 0.001) and did not decline when AI erred. Adult ECG foundation models require pediatric adaptation; fine-tuning offers a data-efficient route to scalable pediatric ECG AI.

title: RIVER: Evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval for enzyme--reaction discovery
summary: Enzyme function annotation and the identification of candidate enzymes for a given reaction are essential steps in connecting genomic information to biochemical reaction networks. However, existing methods rely on sequence or structural similarity or on training with known enzyme--reaction pairs, making it difficult to integrate biochemical evidence across large candidate spaces; they also struggle with retrieval tasks involving enzyme families whose members are highly similar. Here, we introduce RIVER (Reaction--enzyme Inference via Evidence-guided Retrieval), a multi-agent framework for bidirectional enzyme--reaction retrieval that identifies potentially catalyzed reactions for a given enzyme and ranks candidate enzymes for a given reaction. RIVER coordinates large language models, specialized biochemical computational tools, and external knowledge resources to assemble evidence at multiple levels, including reaction chemistry, protein sequences and domains, catalytic mechanisms, and database annotations. Dedicated validation modules further examine evidence gaps and potential conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records. On public benchmarks, RIVER achieves the highest success rates in both enzyme retrieval and enzyme annotation. In family-specific enzyme retrieval, RIVER outperforms the evaluated baselines on the selected datasets and metrics. In Escherichia coli enzyme retrieval tasks constructed from recent literature, RIVER achieves the best retrieval results with closed-source and open-source model configurations, substantially outperforming closed-source general-purpose and biology-specialized multi-agent systems, including Claude Code, Codex, and Phylo Max. These results suggest that evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval can prioritize biochemically supported enzyme--reaction relationships, providing a basis for subsequent experimental validation.

title: Cognitive Tours: Making Understanding a Deliverable in AI-Assisted Development
comment: 6 pages, shorter version submitted to ICSE 2027 Demo Track (under review)
summary: Generative AI and agentic coding are accelerating software development, leading to concerns about technical debt. But two less visible forms of debt, cognitive debt and intent debt, are emerging as key risks to software health. Cognitive debt is the absence or erosion of a team's shared understanding where no one can confidently explain how a system works or predict the impact of a change. Intent debt is the lack of clearly articulated goals, constraints, and rationale that explain what the system is for and guide how it should evolve. This paper presents Cognitive Tours, a tool designed to mitigate and repair cognitive and intent debt. Cognitive Tours is a web-based prototype for creating and following curated paths connecting user needs, design decisions, code, tests, and open questions. AI-assisted skills help audit existing waypoints and tours for possible problems or staleness and suggest candidates for new ones; humans decide what matters, verify relationships, and construct the narrative. This division of work deliberately preserves productive friction: the sensemaking involved in selecting, explaining, and revising a tour, which is intended to foster and share understanding. Our demonstration uses a tour of Cognitive Tours itself to introduce the tool and illustrate its design decisions and interaction mechanisms. A proposed evaluation agenda concludes the paper. A demo is available at https://cognitive-tours-demo.vercel.app/

title: The Intrusion Pathway: How Non-Evidential Context Degrades Language Model Performance
comment: 32 pages, 25 figures, 29 tables. Dikshant Kukreja and Gautam Gupta contributed equally. Website: https://dk4248.github.io/the-intrusion-pathway/ Code: https://github.com/dk4248/the-intrusion-pathway
summary: Language models lose accuracy when a prompt contains non-evidential context: irrelevant statements from unrelated domains, or random off-distribution tokens, with no competing answer and no semantic overlap with the query. Such noise pervades retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and long-context deployments, yet the failure has lacked a mechanistic account. We trace the corruption to the Intrusion Pathway, which starts with MLPs enriching both query-subject and irrelevant-token representations, parroting heads carry prefix-token content to the prediction position, and relational readers largely avoid unrelated sources. Nevertheless, preserved subject enrichment and selective reading do not prevent intrusion in the broader computation. We then localize part of this interference to a sparse set of attention heads, which we call intrusion heads. Their prefix-derived writes promote distractor-related content, while their reduced support for the correct answer arises primarily from weaker non-prefix contributions rather than direct suppression by the prefix. The same heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely weight-disjoint from the heads that integrate relevant contextual evidence, enabling a class-conditional intervention. Replacing the corrupted last-token residual with its clean counterpart, an oracle probe that requires a matched clean forward pass, recovers 97.6% on average of the distractor-induced drop across four downstream tasks. A deployable mask level knockout of about ten heads, roughly 1% of the model's attention heads, recovers 57% at bounded cost to helpful context.

title: RetryBench: Separating Retry Permission from Recovery Outcomes in GPT Tool Use
comment: LLM agents, tool use, idempotency, retry, failure recovery, evaluation, prompt sensitivity, position bias, reliability
summary: LLM agents that call external tools must decide what to do when a tool call times out: retrying risks duplicate side effects, while not retrying can leave the task incomplete. We present RetryBench, an evaluation protocol for retry decisions and failure recovery in tool-using LLM agents.
